newsitem.title: UK: Britain accused of coverup in E-coli report.
newsitem.headline: Britain accused of coverup in E-coli report.

text.p: Britain's Conservative government faced new accusations of incompetence over food safety on Thursday following charges that it suppressed a damaging report on unhealthy conditions in the country's abattoirs.

The report, by the government's Meat Hygiene Service, was leaked to the Financial Times newspaper but was never officially published. It concluded that the abattoirs were becoming breeding grounds for the E-coli organism that killed at least 20 people through food poisoning in Scotland.

"If the recommendations in the report were being implemented uniformly and fully across the country, the risk from E-coli 0157 would be considerably diminished," Robert Swann, the editor of the report, told the newspaper.
The opposition Labour Party, favoured to win an election expected to be held on May 1, said the 1995 report could have helped save lives. They have demanded an explanation from the government.

Members of the inspection team which prepared the report said Ministry of Agriculture officials had told them to tone down some their findings which would have been very damaging to the meat industry.

The report, which was due to be published early last year, was held back after they refused. It would have coincided with the government's admission of a possible link between mad cow disease, or Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), and its human equivalent Creutzfeld-Jakob disease (CJD).
The crisis over mad cow disease resulted in a European Union worldwide ban on British beef exports and crippled the British beef industry, costing it 3.5 billion pounds ($5.7 million).
"The report was perhaps considered unsuitable for publication at the time because the industry was being rocked by the BSE scandal and it would perhaps represent bad timing," Swann said.
Junior Agriculture Minister Angela Browning defended the government's handling of the report, saying it was not meant for public consumption.
"This particular document has been made available to people within the industry. It is an internal document," she told BBC radio.

Professor Hugh Pennington, who is looking into the E-coli outbreak in Scotland, admitted he was not pleased that he had not been told about the findings which could have helped him in his investigation.
"The details of this particular report have not been drawn to our attention," he said. "I'm a bit annoyed. It is an issue everybody knows we are looking at."
